parts: Lesson 8: Indian Architecture as Tourist Attractions — Summary

Indian architecture grew through the ages under dynasties, regional traditions and external influences, and shows the cultural diversity of the country. Order: Harappan, Vedic, Buddhist and Jain, Mauryan, Gupta, rock-cut and free-standing temples, medieval Indo-Islamic (Sultanate, regional kingdoms, Mughal) and colonial and modern styles.

Harappan cities (Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Kalibangan, Surkotada, Lothal) had grid-pattern town planning, roads cutting at right angles, a citadel on high ground, an advanced drainage system, public baths, pillared halls and dwelling houses of well-baked bricks laid in gypsum mortar that survived five thousand years. Lothal (Gujarat) has a dockyard. The bronze dancing girl of Mohenjodaro and a terracotta yogic figure show sculpting skill. The Vedic Aryans used wood, bamboo and reeds (so nothing survives); their most important feature was the fire altar; they used wood along with brick and stone.

Buddhists and Jains built stupas, viharas (monasteries) and chaityas (congregational halls). Buddha's four stupa sites: Lumbini (birth), Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (Mahaparinirvana). Under the Mauryas (322–182 BCE) and Ashoka, polished monolithic stone pillars with animal capitals carried the Dhamma; each weighs about 50 tonnes and stands about 50 ft; the lion capital of the Sarnath pillar is the national emblem. The stupas of Sanchi and Sarnath symbolise Mauryan achievement; Sanchi's gateways show Jataka scenes. Gandhara art blended Greek and Indian art. Nagarjunakonda is another Buddhist site. More than a thousand caves were excavated between the 2nd century BCE and 10th century CE (Ajanta, Ellora, Udaygiri). Rock-cut temples: the chaitya at Karle, the Kailash temple at Ellora (Rashtrakutas) and the ratha temples of Mahabalipuram (Pallavas).

Free-standing Hindu temples began in the Gupta period (Deogarh, Bhitargaon) with a garbhagriha. Dravida style (south): vimana or shikhara, high walls and a gopuram gateway; Pallava shore temple at Mahabalipuram, Kailashnath and Vaikuntha Perumal at Kanchipuram, the Chola Brihadeshwara temple at Tanjore, Belur and Halebid. Nagara style (north and east): shikharas (spiral roofs), garbhagriha and mandap; Lingaraja, Mukteshwara and Jagannath (Odisha); the Sun Temple at Konark (13th century, Narasimha Deva I, a twelve-wheeled chariot for Surya); the Khajuraho temples (Chandellas, 10th–11th century, Kandariya Mahadev). Dilwara temples at Mount Abu (Jain, white marble, Solanki patronage).

The Turks brought domes, arches and minarets and used local craftsmen, so Islamic and indigenous styles blended. Delhi Sultanate: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and Qutub Minar (70 m, five storeys), Alai Darwaza and Hauz Khas (Alauddin Khalji), the strong Tughlaq forts and tombs, the tombs of Ibrahim Lodi and Sher Shah (Sasaram). Regional kingdoms: Ahmedabad (Jama Masjid, Sidi Saiyyad), Mandu (Jahaz Mahal, Hindola Mahal), Deccan (Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur has the largest dome; Golconda fort), Bengal (Adina mosque), Jaunpur (Atala mosque), Hampi of Vijayanagar.

Mughals: Humayun's Tomb (red stone, in a garden, precursor of the Taj), Akbar's forts at Agra and Fatehpur Sikri with the Buland Darwaza (about 41 m, built after the Gujarat victory), Itimad-ud-daula's marble tomb, and Shah Jahan's marble buildings with pietra dura inlay: the Red Fort, Jama Masjid and the Taj Mahal (dome, four minarets, gateway and gardens). Mughal gardens: Shalimar at Kashmir and Lahore.

Portuguese churches in Goa (Basilica of Bom Jesus, St Francis); British Greek and Roman colonnades (Parliament House, Connaught Place), Rashtrapati Bhavan by Lutyens (sandstone with jaali and canopies), the Victoria Memorial (marble, now a museum) and Writers' Building in Kolkata, St Paul's Cathedral (Gothic), Victoria Terminus (now Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus) and the Gateway of India (Indo-Saracenic, yellow basalt, 1924) in Mumbai. After 1947: Le Corbusier designed Chandigarh; Joseph Allen Stein designed the India International Centre; modern Indian architects include Raj Rewal and Charles Correa.

Town planning goes back to about 2350 BCE. There were 2,837 towns in 1594 (qasbas as small towns). The British built port towns (Panaji 1510, Bombay 1532, Madras 1639, Calcutta 1690), railways from 1853, hill stations (Mussoorie, Shimla, Nainital, Darjeeling, Shillong, Nilgiris, Kodaikanal) and Civil Lines and cantonments. Delhi has at least seven old cities: Indraprastha (Yudhishthira), Lal Kot (Anang Pal Tomar), Mehrauli (Prithviraj Chauhan), Siri (Alauddin Khalji), Tughlaqabad (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq), Jahanpanah (Muhammad bin Tughlaq), Firozabad (Firoz Shah), Dinpanah (Humayun) and Shahjahanabad (Shah Jahan). It became the capital of British India in 1911 and New Delhi was completed by 1932. Howrah Bridge (over the Hooghly) is a symbol of Kolkata; Mumbai's Gateway of India and CST and Chennai's High Court, Fort St George and Church of St John are tourist sites.
